place: Fontana del Pantheon, Piazza della Rotonda, Rome: the inscribed base of the obelisk fountain, with its dolphins
how_known: Read at 2000 px: 'CLEMENS XI / PONT·MAX· / FONTIS ET FORI / ORNAMENTO / ANNO SAL· / MDCCXI / PONTIF·XI' on the marble panel, 'RESTAURATA-1974' cut into the step below, the dolphin spouts of Giacomo della Porta's basin. Clement XI set the Macuteo obelisk on the Pantheon fountain in 1711; that inscription is on that fountain only. Lettering correct Latin, consistent serifs.
caption_proposed: The Pantheon fountain: a claim cut in 1711, the restoration dated 1974 beneath it. A source and a date, as every mark here carries.
subject_note: the inscribed marble panel, from 'CLEMENS XI' to 'PONTIF·XI'
text_is_subject: the inscription panel (inside the subject box); 'RESTAURATA-1974' sits at the bottom edge, centre, not in a corner
corners: TL: pale sky and an ochre palazzo; TR: palazzo windows and a pigeon on the cornice; BL: water jet and the basin rim; BR: a carved dolphin. No mark, logo, wordmark or watermark
ai_signs: none: the Latin is correct and spaced like cut letters, the stone stains run with gravity, the pigeons and the water jet are real motion
why: The how-to page says a mark means 'this specific claim is checkable', and the Book carries what lasts while the Field Sheet carries the dated revision. Rome does the same in stone: a statement with its author and its year, then a dated restoration. The fountain is the reader's first evidence that facts here come with a source. It is not the Pantheon twice: p65 prints the rotunda's interior through the doors, and this frame shows the fountain base in the square outside, with no part of the temple in it. 9504 px native across 816 px printed is 11.6x.

Two true frames, both killed. #8 is Via del Corso running straight to the Vittoriano (the Corso links Piazza del Popolo to Piazza Venezia, the book's centre, which proves the walk). But at 100% it carries shop and brand lettering: 'Pepe Jeans' and a 'CHANGE' exchange sign on the left, an 'AW LAB' sign on the right, and a vertical HOTEL sign. Its smiling foreground face is sharp too. Cropping to the closing window cannot lose them. #6 (Trajan's Column and Santa Maria di Loreto at the edge of Piazza Venezia) is a monument, and monuments are full at 3 (pp. 31, 49, 62). The rest are the Pantheon (#1, #9, already the p65 subject), the Spanish Steps (#2, #7) and Navona (#5, killed earlier as adding nothing). Stays typographic: the chapter's name on the red field.

place: Barberini station, Line A, Rome metro: the southbound platform, a train arriving
how_known: Read at 2000 px: 'BARBERINI' on the red band of the tunnel wall (right) and on the orange platform wall (left). These are Line A's orange station finishes and its white CAF train with the red stripe. Barberini is the Line A stop on the core's north-east edge.
caption_proposed: Line A at Barberini, on the core's edge: the train for the Vatican hop, not for the centre it curves around.
subject_note: the arriving train's front and its run of carriages; the 'BARBERINI' band at x≈0.86 is the frame's identifying text
text_is_subject: 'BARBERINI' station-name band, right wall, just outside the train box, not in a corner
corners: TL: platform ceiling lights and the orange wall; TR: corrugated tunnel lining; BL: a rider's back and backpack, face turned away; BR: tunnel wall and track. No mark, logo or text. The overhead screen shows a car advert with no legible lettering
ai_signs: none: real motion blur on the train only, the platform tactile strip consistent, signage spelled correctly
why: The chapter's case is that the metro is a tool for three journeys out of the core and a hole in the middle of it. A Line A platform at the edge of the centre makes that call physical: the network is real and fast, and it is somewhere else. No face is sharp toward the camera: the riders stand side-on or with their backs turned, most of them masked. This is the book's one transit frame from p4 to p27, so the TAP (d02) and €55 (d03) closings cannot also take a transit picture, and none was found for them anyway. Native 6240 px over 816 px is 7.6x.

Not Rome: Siena (#4, Via S. Agata with the Torre del Mangia), Como (#7), Milan (#9, San Lorenzo's columns), a 'Castello della Madonna' plaque (#1), a seaside town (#2), a hill town (#6). The Roman lanes (#3, #8) cannot be placed, so '13′' would sit over an unnamed street: the old d01 lanes died of that. Typographic, '13′' in gold on the ink field.

Two searches ('rome metro turnstile contactless; atac ticket validator rome', then 'rome metro ticket barrier; metro roma tornelli') turned up no contactless reader or ATAC gate. The paper tickets in hand (#5, #8, #9) show what the call tells you not to buy. The trains repeat the Barberini frame on p15, inside 12 pages. Typographic: 'TAP.' in gold on the ink field.

The Gallery of Maps (#2, #8) is the Museums inside, not a line. The dome and nave (#1, #5) say nothing about the two lines. The p87 'queue round the square' margin has the same lack. Typographic.

place: Galleria Borghese, Sala degli Imperatori, Rome: Bernini's Rape of Proserpina (Pluto and Proserpina)
how_known: Read at 2000 px: Bernini's marble group of the crowned, curly-bearded Pluto lifting Proserpina, her hand pushing against his face. Behind it, the room's gilded vault with grisaille medallions, the coloured-marble wall revetment and the blue-ground hexagonal reliefs of the Sala degli Imperatori, where the group stands. The work is unique and fixed in that room.
caption_proposed: Bernini's Pluto and Proserpina in the Galleria Borghese: no walk-ins, ever. One of the three you book the day your dates are firm.
verdict_of: the Borghese as one of the three sights that sell out
subject_note: the marble group, from Pluto's crown and Proserpina's raised hand down to the cut at the bottom edge; the vault above is clear
corners: TL: gilded cornice and painted vault; TR: painted vault; BL: marble wall panel and a column capital; BR: putti relief and gilded frame. No mark, logo, text, label or visitor
ai_signs: none: Bernini's carving read correctly (the hand on the cheek, the crown), vault ornament regular and continuous, no melted or repeated motifs
why: The killed p34 frame was this sculpture printed under the Vatican's 'TWO LINES', the wrong chapter. Here it is the manual's own example: the Borghese is the strictest of the three that sell out, with a mandatory slot, a hard cap and no walk-ins. Set the '3' in the vault, upper right (source x ≥ 0.62, y ≤ 0.45), clear of both heads, so the verdict never touches the subject. It is not a twice: no Borghese frame survives anywhere. The interior category is new to the book. p37's St Peter's Square sits on the facing page, so if the p37 ruling moves that frame to Decision 05's closing (p34), the two keep a page between them. 5013 px native across 816 px is 6.1x.

Every frame is a branded card terminal (Square, SumUp and others) on studio tables, with no place and no EUR/USD prompt on any screen: the same 'blank terminal' fault that killed the old d07 card-reader. Typographic: '€' in gold on the ink field.

#7 is the Tazza d'Oro, a named business with its sign, and the book names none. #8 is a crowded street with BAR and GELATERIA signs and faces sharp. #6 and #1 are night terraces that cannot be placed. #2-#4 and #9 are lanes that cannot be placed, and none of them shows the ninety seconds. '90″' would sit over a street it does not name. Typographic.

place: no_place: a lane paved in sampietrini in central Rome. The frame proves the paving, not a street
how_known: Read at 2000x3000: the square-cut basalt setts laid in fan-shaped courses, worn smooth and uneven, cut by a drain grille. Around them, Roman palazzo walls with travertine string-courses, wall lanterns and black-and-white bollards. The street is not named in the frame, so the caption claims the stone, not the address.
caption_proposed: Sampietrini underfoot, lane after lane: the stone the walking shoes are broken in for.
subject_note: the cobbled roadway from the bollards to the bottom edge (a band: printed whole, never cropped)
corners: TL: dark palazzo wall and shutters; TR: palazzo wall, an air-conditioning unit; BL: setts; BR: setts and the edge of some cardboard. No mark, logo or legible text in any corner. A vertical 'GARAGE' sign and tags of graffiti sit mid-frame, illegible at 264 px
ai_signs: none: every sett is different and lit by a single source, the perspective is continuous, the far figures are small and natural
why: The before-you-fly line says 'real walking shoes, broken in. Rome's sampietrini cobblestones are hard on feet and footwear'. This proves it: the paving takes up the whole lower half of the frame. It is also the book's own sign, the sampietrino from the cover ('ONE STONE IS WHERE YOU SLEEP'). The figures are far down the lane, so there are no faces. It is not 'a lane that proves nothing': the paving is the claim, and the caption names it. Printed whole at 264 px wide; 3648 px native is 13.8x. #9 was set aside for a legible licence plate on the right-hand scooter.

place: Vatican Museums, Vatican City: Giuseppe Momo's double-helix spiral stair (1932), seen from the top
how_known: Read at 2000 px: the bronze balustrade cast with acanthus and putti and the papal arms of Pius XI (top centre), the ramped stair of white-edged treads winding to the round floor with its central post, and the green marble lining. This is Momo's stair at the Vatican Museums, and it is unique. The visitors are tiny and seen from above.
caption_proposed: The Momo stair at the Vatican Museums: the Vatican is its own half-day, booked early, and it never shares one with the Forum.
subject_note: the inner turns of the spiral, from the second balustrade ring to the floor
corners: TL: bronze balustrade relief; TR: balustrade and green marble; BL: balustrade relief; BR: grey stair surface and yellow safety lines (floor paint, no lettering). No mark, logo or legible text; the balustrade's small cast lettering is illegible even at 2000 px
ai_signs: none: the relief repeats as cast bronze does, the people are small and consistent with the height, the perspective spiral is continuous
why: The plan's whole rule is two heavy half-days that never share a day. The Forum closes Decision 04 on p31, and this is the other half, the Vatican on its booked early slot (p68-p69). Using one of the Vatican Museums' recognised interiors on the plan's closing balances the Forum frame without repeating St Peter's Square (p37). The caption claims no exit route, since the stair's use varies. The interior category appears twice (p38, p69), 31 pages apart. It is not golden. 5931 px native is 7.3x.

place: Orvieto Cathedral (Duomo di Orvieto), Umbria: the central portal's lunette, with the marble Madonna and Child under Lorenzo Maitani's bronze angels and canopy
how_known: Read at 2000 px: the Cosmatesque-inlaid archivolts with twisted marble colonnettes, and in the lunette the seated marble Madonna and Child flanked by bronze angels drawing back a bronze baldachin. That is Maitani's group over the main door of Orvieto's Duomo, unique to it. Orvieto is named in this chapter (p71: one hour by direct train, 'crowned by one of Italy's most spectacular Gothic cathedrals').
caption_proposed: The central portal of Orvieto's cathedral, an hour out by direct train: the near name, not the famous one.
subject_note: the lunette group: Madonna, Child, the two bronze angels and the canopy
corners: TL: inlaid archivolt; TR: inlaid archivolt; BL: twisted colonnettes and the lintel; BR: colonnettes and a pigeon. No mark, logo, text or watermark
ai_signs: none: heavy HDR toning (real processing, not generation); the inlay pattern is irregular as hand-cut work, the pigeons are real, the iconography is correct
why: The chapter's verdict is to resist the famous day trip (Pompeii, Florence) and take a near one: Ostia, the Castelli, Orvieto, Tivoli. Ostia already closes Decision 09 on p49, so the day-trips closing shows another near one, the cathedral the text names. This replaces the killed Naples/Vesuvius frame, which showed the famous day trip the page argues against. A church, not a ruin, so the monument budget is untouched. There is no sky and it is not golden. 3000 px native over 816 px is 3.7x, the smallest pick but above 1.5x.

place: The Spanish Steps (Scalinata di Trinità dei Monti), Piazza di Spagna, Rome, looking up to Trinità dei Monti and the Sallustiano obelisk
how_known: Read at 2000 px: the twin-towered façade of Trinità dei Monti with its two clock faces and Latin frieze, the obelisk before it, the travertine flights with their curved balustrades and the inscribed plaque on the middle landing, the palm on the right terrace. Only Piazza di Spagna has this view.
caption_proposed: The Spanish Steps with no one sitting: climb them, walk down them, but sit and you are moved on.
subject_note: the church façade, the obelisk and the central flights down to the landing
corners: TL: ochre palazzo and shutters; TR: sky and a sliver of building; BL: travertine treads; BR: travertine treads. No mark, logo, sign or text
ai_signs: none: the frieze lettering is coherent Latin, the treads wear unevenly, there is one real figure with a consistent shadow
why: Failure modes names one place: 'Sitting on the Spanish Steps. Banned and enforced'. The previous p79 frame (the Roma Pass on a table) showed what the book tells you not to buy. This one shows the rule obeyed: the only person on the steps is walking down. The caption claims the rule, not why the steps are empty. The figure is a small mid-ground walker on a page that is not a pickpocket page, and his face is not sharp at print size. The Spanish Steps appear nowhere else among the frames. Pale sky with the sun not visible, so not golden. 5043 px is 6.2x.

The page's fountain is one 'you didn't plan to see, running in an empty square'. The Trevi (#1, #2, #8, #9) is the most planned fountain in Rome. #1 shows it with nobody in frame, but the source cuts the attic statues at the top, and an empty Trevi would be a claim the caption cannot make. #7 is Piazza della Rotonda at night: true, but with English menu boards, a 'CHANGE' sign and tables on the famous piazza, the very trap Decision 08 warns against. #6 is St Peter's Square (printed p37). #3-#5 are the Spanish Steps by night, inside 12 pages of p79. The essay closes on its name on the red field.

The Pompeii streets with Vesuvius (#3, #6) are true, but they would print the famous day trip on the page that argues against it (the Naples kill on p72 had the same fault). They would also be a fourth ancient monument, facing Ostia on p49. Left to the stack.
